title: Real Estate Finance I: Instruments & Foreclosure
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: The three parties to a California deed of trust are the:
rationales: Mortgagor and mortgagee are the two parties to a mortgage; escrow is not a party to the security instrument.
Correct. The trustor is the borrower, the beneficiary is the lender, and the trustee holds bare legal title with the power of sale.
Grantor and grantee are deed terms, not the parties to a deed of trust.
Vendor and vendee describe seller and buyer under a land contract.

questions.stem: Which statement about the promissory note and the deed of trust is TRUE?
options: The note secures the deed of trust
The deed of trust is the evidence of the debt
The security instrument follows the note when the note is sold
Both must be recorded to be valid
rationales: The relationship runs the other way — the deed of trust secures the note.
The note is the evidence of the debt; the deed of trust is the collateral.
Correct. The security follows the note automatically, which is why a borrower's loan servicer can change without any new security instrument.
The note is generally not recorded, and recording is not required for validity between the parties.

questions.stem: California is a lien theory state, which means that when a borrower signs a deed of trust, the lender:
options: Receives legal title until the loan is repaid
Receives a lien against the property while the borrower retains ownership
Becomes a co-owner with the borrower
rationales: The trustee holds bare legal title as a technical device; the lender does not take title.
Correct. In a lien theory state the lender holds a lien, the borrower retains ownership and possession, and a loan therefore does not sever a joint tenancy.
No co-ownership arises from a loan.
The borrower keeps possession throughout.

questions.stem: The document recorded to clear a paid-off deed of trust from title is a:
rationales: A satisfaction of mortgage clears a mortgage, the two-party instrument uncommon in California.
Correct. Upon payoff the beneficiary requests, and the trustee records, a deed of reconveyance releasing the lien.
A trustee's deed conveys title to the buyer at a foreclosure sale.
A notice of completion relates to mechanics' lien deadlines.

questions.stem: The recorded document that begins a non-judicial foreclosure and starts the reinstatement period is the:
rationales: The Notice of Sale comes later, after the reinstatement period expires.
Correct. Recording the Notice of Default starts the roughly three-month reinstatement period and places the default in the public record.
A lis pendens gives notice of pending litigation affecting title.
An abstract of judgment creates a judgment lien.

questions.stem: A borrower wants to stop foreclosure two months after the Notice of Default was recorded. To reinstate the loan, the borrower must pay:
options: The delinquent amounts plus costs and fees
One year of future payments in advance
rationales: Paying the entire balance is redemption, required only after the reinstatement period expires.
Correct. Reinstatement means curing the arrears plus costs and fees, after which the loan continues on its original terms.
No advance-payment requirement exists.
The sale price is irrelevant to reinstatement.

questions.stem: Following a completed non-judicial trustee's sale in California, the former owner's statutory right of redemption is:
rationales: One year is the judicial foreclosure redemption period where a deficiency was sought.
Three months is the judicial redemption period where the sale satisfied the debt.
Ninety days corresponds to no California post-trustee-sale right.
Correct. There is no post-sale statutory redemption after a trustee's sale — once the sale concludes, the borrower's interest is extinguished.

questions.stem: A lender forecloses non-judicially on an investment fourplex and the sale leaves a $60,000 shortfall. The lender may:
options: Obtain a deficiency judgment, because the property was not owner-occupied
Not obtain a deficiency judgment, because non-judicial foreclosure bars it entirely
Obtain a deficiency judgment within 90 days of the sale
Obtain a deficiency judgment only with the Commissioner's approval
rationales: Owner-occupancy matters to the separate purchase-money bar, but the trustee's-sale bar applies regardless of property type.
Correct. No deficiency judgment is permitted after any non-judicial foreclosure — the lender traded that right for speed when it chose the trustee's sale.
There is no 90-day deficiency window after a trustee's sale.
The Commissioner has no role in deficiency actions.

questions.stem: Which loan retains California's purchase-money anti-deficiency protection?
options: A cash-out refinance on an owner-occupied home
A loan used to buy an owner-occupied single-family home
A commercial loan on a retail center
A HELOC used to consolidate credit card debt
rationales: A cash-out refinance is generally not purchase-money and can lose the protection in a judicial foreclosure.
Correct. A loan used to purchase a one-to-four unit owner-occupied dwelling — including seller carry-back financing — is protected from deficiency even in judicial foreclosure.
Commercial property is outside the owner-occupied dwelling protection.
A HELOC used for debt consolidation was not used to purchase the property.

questions.stem: A first trust deed forecloses. A second trust deed and a later judgment lien are recorded against the property. After the sale, the junior liens are:
options: Extinguished from title by the senior foreclosure
Unaffected and still enforceable against the property
rationales: Correct. Foreclosure by a senior lienholder wipes junior liens from title, though the underlying debts may survive as unsecured claims subject to anti-deficiency rules.
The bidder takes free of the wiped junior liens.
Junior liens are eliminated, not promoted.
The liens no longer attach to the property after the senior's sale.

questions.stem: A trustee's sale by the FIRST trust deed holder nets $465,000. Delinquent taxes are $11,500, the foreclosing first is $402,000, a 2021 second is $70,000, and a 2023 judgment lien is $25,000. The second trust deed holder receives:
rationales: There are insufficient proceeds to pay the second in full.
Correct. 465,000 − 11,500 (taxes) − 402,000 (first) = $51,500 available to the second, leaving it $18,500 short.
$63,000 corresponds to no step in the priority distribution.
Funds do remain for the second after taxes and the foreclosing first are paid.

questions.stem: An interest-only note of $420,000 bears 6.75% annual interest. The monthly interest payment is:
rationales: $2,835 divides the annual interest by 10 rather than 12.
$28,350 is the annual interest, not the monthly payment.
$3,150 corresponds to a 9% rate.

questions.stem: Using a 360-day banker's year, interest accruing over 73 days on a $420,000 note at 6.75% is:
rationales: Correct. Annual interest = $28,350; daily = 28,350 ÷ 360 = $78.75; × 73 days = $5,748.75.
$5,670 uses a 365-day year daily rate applied incorrectly.
$78.75 is the daily interest, not the 73-day total.
$2,362.50 is one month's interest.

questions.stem: The clause permitting a lender to declare the entire loan balance immediately due upon the borrower's default is the:
rationales: An alienation clause is triggered by transfer of the property, not by default.
Correct. The acceleration clause makes the whole balance due on default, and every foreclosure depends on it.
A subordination clause changes lien priority.
A release clause frees individual parcels from a blanket loan.

questions.stem: A lender may call a loan due when the borrower sells the property because of the:
rationales: Acceleration is triggered by default; here the borrower is current but transferring.
Correct. The alienation, or due-on-sale, clause lets the lender call the balance due upon transfer, which is why most modern loans cannot simply be assumed without consent.
A prepayment clause addresses early payoff, not transfer.
A defeasance clause concerns defeating the security upon payment.

questions.stem: A buyer takes title 'subject to' the seller's existing loan rather than assuming it. As to the note, the SELLER:
options: Is liable only for one year
rationales: Only an assumption with novation releases the original borrower.
Correct. Taking subject to leaves the original borrower fully liable on the note, and the loan's alienation clause may also let the lender accelerate upon the transfer.
No guarantor status is created; the seller's original promise stands.
Liability does not expire after a year.

questions.stem: A borrower with a $480,000 first and a $95,000 HELOC offers the first lender a deed in lieu of foreclosure. The lender will most likely refuse because:
options: A deed in lieu requires court approval
Accepting the deed means taking the property subject to the junior HELOC, whereas foreclosure would extinguish it
Deeds in lieu are prohibited in California
The borrower would retain a right of redemption
rationales: No court approval is required for a deed in lieu.
Correct. A deed in lieu takes the property subject to junior liens, while foreclosure wipes them out — so a lender facing a second lien rationally chooses foreclosure.
Deeds in lieu are lawful; lenders simply often decline them.
A deed in lieu is a voluntary conveyance, not a foreclosure creating redemption rights.

questions.stem: At a trustee's sale, the foreclosing beneficiary may bid up to the amount owed without producing cash. This is called a:
rationales: Correct. A credit bid lets the beneficiary offset its bid against the debt owed rather than paying cash, up to the amount of the obligation.
'Short bid' is not a recognized term.
A deficiency is the shortfall after sale, not a bidding method.
Subordination concerns lien priority, not bidding.

questions.stem: A lender chooses judicial foreclosure over a trustee's sale primarily to:
options: Preserve the possibility of a deficiency judgment
Avoid giving the borrower any redemption rights
rationales: Judicial foreclosure is substantially slower, often taking a year or more.
Litigation makes judicial foreclosure more expensive, not less.
Correct. The sole practical advantage is preserving a possible deficiency judgment, which the non-judicial route forfeits entirely.
Judicial foreclosure creates post-sale redemption rights; the trustee's sale is what eliminates them.

questions.stem: A subdivision builder's blanket loan covers 40 lots. The provision allowing individual lots to be freed from the lien as they are sold and paid for is a:
rationales: Subordination changes priority relative to another loan.
Correct. A release clause permits partial reconveyance of individual parcels from a blanket loan so the builder can deliver clear title to each buyer.
Acceleration makes the balance due on default.
An alienation clause lets the lender call the loan on transfer — the opposite of what a builder needs.
